chahohbili.name: Chakhokhbili
chahohbili.description: Chakhokhbili is a fragrant chicken stew that embodies the spirit of a Georgian feast. Tender meat stewed with tomatoes, onion, garlic and plenty of spices has a rich, bright taste. The dish was originally made with pheasant, but today chicken is used. It is served with bread or rice to soak up the sauce.
chahohbili.quote: Chakhokhbili brings the family together at the table; its aroma fills the house with warmth
chahohbili.history: The name comes from khokhobi, meaning pheasant: the dish was originally made with game. Later chicken replaced the pheasant, and tomatoes — now essential to chakhokhbili — entered the recipe relatively recently.
chahohbili.ingredientsText:
Chicken 800 g
Onion 3
Tomatoes 4
Sweet pepper ½
Garlic 3 cloves
Coriander, parsley to taste
Chilli ½
Spices and salt to taste

dolma-armyanskaya.name: Dolma
dolma-armyanskaya.description: Dolma is one of the most refined dishes of Armenian cuisine and a symbol of the hospitality of an Armenian home. Tender, slightly sour grape leaves wrap a filling of rice, minced meat and fragrant herbs. Dolma is served with matsun or garlic sauce and is a must at festive tables and family dinners.
dolma-armyanskaya.quote: Dolma is the art of balance: tender meat, fragrant rice and juicy grape leaves in harmony from the first bite
dolma-armyanskaya.history: Dolma in grape leaves is made across the Caucasus and the Middle East. In Armenia it is called tolma and served with garlic matsun; in summer young leaves are used, and for winter they are pickled.
dolma-armyanskaya.ingredientsText:
Grape leaves 400 g
Beef 600 g
Pork 100 g
Long-grain rice 100 g
Onion 100 g
Fresh basil 20 g
Parsley 20 g
Coriander 20 g
Ground black pepper
Salt

dolma-azerbajdzhanskaya.name: Dolma
dolma-azerbajdzhanskaya.description: Dolma is one of the best-loved dishes of Azerbaijani cuisine, made with great attention to detail. Grape leaves or vegetables (aubergines, tomatoes, peppers) are filled with rice, minced meat and fragrant herbs. Dolma is served with garlic yogurt and is a must on the festive table.
dolma-azerbajdzhanskaya.quote: Azerbaijani dolma is not only grape leaves: it is also made from aubergines, peppers, tomatoes and even fruit such as quince
dolma-azerbajdzhanskaya.history:
The name dolma comes from the Turkic verb doldurmaq, "to fill".

In Azerbaijan dolma comes in many varieties: besides grape leaves, peppers, tomatoes, quince, aubergines and other vegetables and fruit are stuffed.
dolma-azerbajdzhanskaya.ingredientsText:
Minced lamb and beef 100 g
Grape leaves 120 g
Mint, coriander and dill, a little of each
Butter 20 g
Rice 1 tbsp
Onion ¼
Salt and black pepper to taste

gata.name: Gata
gata.description: Gata is a sweet symbol of Armenian cuisine, associated with comfort and the warmth of home. It is a flaky pastry with a filling of butter, flour and sugar, crisp outside and soft inside. Gata can be round like the sun or cut into portions. It is often baked for holidays or simply as a treat with tea, and every region of Armenia has its own recipe.
gata.quote: Every region of Armenia has its own gata recipe, but one thing never changes: it brings people together at the same table
gata.history:
The first written mention of gata dates from the 13th century, though no one knows exactly when the pastry appeared. It has absorbed the national spirit: despite hardships well into the 20th century, Armenians preserved their identity and culture.

Gata is loved both in Armenia and across the diaspora, which has kept the national features of its cuisine far from home.
gata.ingredientsText:
Wheat flour 58 g
Butter 33 g
Matsun yogurt 20 g
Baking soda 1 tsp
A pinch of salt
For the filling: melted butter 13 g, vanilla sugar 1 tsp, wheat flour 40 g, icing sugar 41 g

hachapuri.name: Khachapuri
hachapuri.description: Khachapuri is the hallmark of Georgian cuisine, a cheese bread that wins hearts with its simplicity and rich taste. Thin dough filled with melted sulguni or Imeretian cheese gives the perfect balance of crisp crust and tender filling. Depending on the region, khachapuri is round (Imeretian), boat-shaped (Adjarian) or with cheese on top (Megrelian). It is served hot so the cheese stretches.
hachapuri.quote: Khachapuri is not just a cheese pie but a whole culinary culture: wherever you are in Georgia, it will always find a place on the table
hachapuri.history: Khachapuri is baked all over Georgia, and almost every region has its own version: Imeretian, Megrelian, Adjarian, Gurian. The name is usually explained as "curd bread", from khacho (curd) and puri (bread).
hachapuri.ingredientsText:
Milk 250 ml
Water 250 ml
Fresh yeast 10 g
Sugar 10 g
Salt 5 g
Flour 700 g
Eggs 2
Sunflower oil 120 g
Sulguni 300 g
Imeretian cheese 300 g
Hard cheese 50 g
Butter 100 g

hash.name: Khash
hash.description: Khash is not just a soup: it is a legend of Armenian cuisine, a dish that demands time, patience and respect for tradition. It is made from beef feet simmered for a long time until the meat literally falls off the bone. Khash is served hot with garlic, herbs and dried lavash crumbled straight into the broth. It is traditionally eaten early in the morning, often after long feasts, to restore strength.
hash.quote: Khash is a dish that brings people together. It is traditionally eaten early in the morning to get energy for the whole day
hash.history:
It began as a dish of the poor and later became a symbol of Armenian culture and culinary tradition.

Legend has it that a king who spent the night in a village tried khash and liked it so much that he made it the main dish of his table.
hash.ingredientsText:
Beef feet 1.5 kg
Beef tripe 500 g
Garlic 3 heads
Radish 1

hingalsh.name: Khingalash
hingalsh.description: Khingalash is a distinctive dish of Chechen cuisine: flatbreads of unleavened wheat dough filled with sweet pumpkin. The tender filling goes perfectly with the soft crust, and they are served with melted butter. For softness, the cooked flatbreads have long been dipped in hot water.
hingalsh.quote: The dish is so filling that if a guest eats little, the host may say: "You eat as if you had just had khingalash"
hingalsh.history:
Chechnya has long grown barley, wheat, millet, maize, oats and rice, as well as flax and cotton; barley and wheat are the oldest grains. Dough was made both unleavened and with yeast.

Chechens have long known hop yeast, called khoyakhar. Dough is often soured with sour milk, and fillings are curd cheese, fresh cheese, mashed potato or pumpkin — Chechnya is known for its melon and gourd growing and its livestock.

hinkali.name: Khinkali
hinkali.description: Khinkali are not just Georgian dumplings but a real art. Thin, elastic dough hides a juicy filling of minced meat (usually beef or pork) seasoned with onion, garlic and herbs. The secret is the broth that stays inside, bursting with flavour at the first bite. They are eaten by hand, held by the topknot, which is traditionally left uneaten.
hinkali.quote: Khinkali are a real culinary adventure: every bite comes with a burst of juice and flavour
hinkali.history: Khinkali came from the mountains of eastern Georgia — Pshavi, Khevsureti and Tusheti. The mountain version with chopped meat and spices is called mtiuluri, the town version with herbs kalakuri. They are eaten by hand, holding the topknot, which is then left on the plate.
hinkali.ingredientsText:
Wheat flour 500 g
Water 400 ml
Salt 1½ tsp
Veal 250 g
Beef 250 g
Lard 100 g
Onion 100 g
Garlic 2 cloves
Ground cumin to taste
Chilli to taste
Coriander

horovacz-narsharab.name: Khorovats
horovacz-narsharab.description: Khorovats is a traditional Armenian dish of grilled vegetables, perfect for a barbecue. Vegetables are roasted over coals outdoors, and at home they can be baked in the oven.
horovacz-narsharab.quote: Khorovats is a dish made with soul
horovacz-narsharab.history: The word khorovats means "barbecue" in Armenian. Vegetables for the salad are roasted over coals outdoors, or at home in the oven or over a gas flame. Khorovats is served with kebabs, potatoes, grilled fish or simply with lavash and fresh bread.
horovacz-narsharab.ingredientsText:
Aubergines 3
Tomatoes 3
Sweet peppers 2
Onion 1
Garlic 1 clove
Vegetable oil to taste
Salt
Black pepper
Herbs

kutaby.name: Qutab
kutaby.description: Qutab are thin flatbreads that win you over with their simplicity and refined taste. The filling can be anything from juicy herbs (coriander, dill, spinach) to tender meat or pumpkin. Qutab are cooked on a dry pan until golden and then brushed with melted butter to make them soft. They are served with yogurt or a fermented milk drink. An ideal snack or light supper.
kutaby.quote: Qutab are thin filled flatbreads, made with meat, herbs, pumpkin or cheese and served with yogurt sauces
kutaby.history: The history of qutab goes back to ancient times, when people used leftover bread dough to make this tasty dish.
kutaby.ingredientsText:
Wheat flour 96 g
Refined vegetable oil 1 tbsp
Onion 1
Butter 1 tbsp
Parsley 80 g
Sumac to taste
A pinch of salt

lahmadzho.name: Lahmajo
lahmadzho.description: Lahmajo is the Armenian "pizza", winning people over with its simplicity and rich taste. A thin round of dough is spread with minced meat, tomatoes, onion and spices and baked until crisp. It is often rolled up and eaten with herbs, lemon juice or matsun. A popular street snack and a family favourite.
lahmadzho.quote: Armenians say lahmajo is "food for the soul": simple and rich in taste, it is loved by locals and visitors alike
lahmadzho.history:
In Arab countries the dish is called lahmacun or lahm bi ajin. While waiting for their order, customers watch the dough change in the oven: first it spreads, then it bubbles and rises, all in a few seconds.

Armenians are the largest Christian community in Jordan after Arab Christians, and lahmajo is sold in Armenian bakeries in Amman.
lahmadzho.ingredientsText: For the dough: kefir or matsoni 250 ml, wheat flour 400–450 g, salt ½ tsp

lobio.name: Lobio
lobio.description: Lobio proves that beans can be a true delicacy. Cooked beans dressed with walnuts, garlic, coriander and spices turn into a tender, fragrant mass. Lobio can be served hot or cold, and its texture ranges from a thick purée to whole beans. It is served in clay pots, which adds authenticity and warmth.
lobio.quote: Lobio speaks of Georgian hospitality. It is served with gomi (cornmeal porridge) or simply with lavash
lobio.history: Beans reached the Caucasus from the Americas in the early modern period but quickly became a mainstay of the Georgian table. Lobio is made hot, in a clay pot, and cold with walnuts; it is eaten with mchadi and pickles, especially on fasting days.
lobio.ingredientsText:
Beans – 63 g (red or pinto)
Walnuts – 13 g
Onion – 0.4
Tomato – 0.3
Garlic – 0.4 clove
Coriander – 1.5 g
Khmeli suneli – 0.1 tbsp
Hot red pepper – 0.1
Salt to taste
Vegetable oil – 0.3 tbsp
Black pepper to taste

pahlava.name: Pakhlava
pahlava.description: Pakhlava is the sweet symbol of Azerbaijani cuisine, winning hearts with its layered texture and rich taste. Thin layers of pastry soaked in honey or syrup alternate with a filling of chopped nuts (usually walnuts or hazelnuts). Every piece combines a crisp crust and a tender filling that melts in the mouth. Pakhlava is a must on the festive table, especially at Novruz and other celebrations.
pahlava.quote: Pakhlava is not just a dessert, it is part of the culture. It is made for Novruz, weddings and other celebrations to share joy and gratitude
pahlava.history:
Azerbaijani pakhlava is a many-layered dessert with nuts and syrup that plays an important role in Azerbaijani culture and festivities.

Although historians point to early mentions of pakhlava in Ottoman cookbooks (15th century), Azerbaijan can also claim its share in the history of this dessert.
pahlava.ingredientsText:
For the dough: wheat flour 35 g, milk 12 ml, butter 6 g, 1 egg, sugar 4 g, dry yeast 1 g, salt 1 g
For the filling: walnuts 30 g, butter 8 g, sugar 15 g, potato starch 1 tbsp
For the syrup: honey 10 g, sugar 10 g, water 10 ml, lemon juice 1 tbsp

plov.name: Pilaf
plov.description: Pilaf is the king of Azerbaijani cuisine, combining a wealth of flavours and traditions. Steamed rice is served with fragrant meat (most often lamb), dried fruit, chestnuts and spices. Each part is cooked separately and then brought together. Pilaf is a symbol of hospitality, served at big celebrations and family dinners.
plov.quote: Saffron is the secret of the golden colour and unique aroma of Azerbaijani pilaf: it is added to the rice so that every grain shines like a jewel
plov.history:
Pilaf, like many Eastern dishes, has its roots in ancient Persia and Central Asia, where rice was cooked with meat and spices.

Pilaf spread across the East along trade routes and with military campaigns, reaching Azerbaijan, whose cuisine has many kinds of pilaf that differ in method and ingredients.
plov.ingredientsText:
Onion 4 large
Raisins ½ cup
Dried apricots 1 cup
Prunes ½ cup
Chestnuts 500 g
A pinch of cinnamon
Butter 400–600 g
For the gazmakh crust: flour ½ cup, egg, kefir

saczivi.name: Satsivi
saczivi.description: Satsivi is a refined dish served cold, with a complex texture and taste. The sauce is made of walnuts ground with garlic, spices and vinegar into a thick, velvety mass. Boiled chicken or turkey is added and left to infuse so that all the flavours blend. Satsivi is a must on the Georgian festive table.
saczivi.quote: Satsivi is a Christmas dish of walnuts, coriander and spices that symbolises abundance and joy
saczivi.history: The name relates to tsiva, meaning cold: satsivi is served chilled. It is one of the main dishes of the Georgian New Year table, made with chicken, turkey or fried vegetables.
saczivi.ingredientsText:
Chicken or turkey, up to 2 kg
Butter 20 g
Onion 1 kg
Coriander 4 sprigs
Shelled walnuts 600 g
Black pepper 1 tbsp
Ground coriander 1 tbsp
Imeretian saffron 1 tbsp
Cloves 3–6
A pinch of cinnamon
Garlic 4–8 cloves
White wine vinegar 1 tbsp
Salt to taste

shah-plov.name: Shah pilaf
shah-plov.description: Shah pilaf is a gem of Azerbaijani cuisine that amazes with its beauty and taste. Rice is laid in a "crown" wrapped in a crisp crust of lavash. Inside are tender meat, dried fruit and nuts. Shah pilaf is a dish for special occasions and a symbol of the wealth and generosity of the Azerbaijani table.
shah-plov.quote: Shah pilaf is not just food but a show: it is brought out whole and cut in front of the guests
shah-plov.history:
Shah pilaf (also called khan pilaf or "royal pilaf") is a festive Azerbaijani dish known for its unusual method and presentation.

Its history is tied to the Azerbaijani culinary tradition, in which pilaf holds a special place.
shah-plov.ingredientsText:
Beef 600 g
Rice 600 g
Ghee 350 g
Onion 250 g
Dried apricots 150 g
Golden raisins 150 g
Dried cherry plums 100 g
Boiled chestnuts 150 g
Turmeric
Saffron 3–5 threads
Salt
Barberries 50 g (optional)
Thin lavash 400 g
